channel.title: Joyce Ma
channel.description: Joyce Ma's personal column: pre-class prep and after-class notes from Harvard Business School's OPM program, plus essays on books, AI and life.

item.title: HBS Notes | Marketing: Das's Unit 3 Wrap-Up — A promise takes the whole organization to keep
item.description: The final session: a summary of Unit 3's concepts, with Starbucks Korea as optional reading.

item.title: HBS Prep | Leadership: Mudo — What kind of empowerment does a transformation need
item.description: A founder hopes his company can keep running without him, and still waits every day for the sales figures. Mudo's transformation took place while both of these wishes were alive at once.

item.title: HBS Prep | Leadership: Jean-Claude Biver — Giving an old craft new meaning
item.description: Jean-Claude Biver (A): The Reemergence of the Swiss Watch Industry.

item.title: HBS Prep | Operations: Shohei Ohtani — Bringing ambition into every day
item.description: A teenage boy writes down an enormous dream — and also writes down tidying his room, thanking people, and building lower-body strength. What draws me to Shohei Ohtani's goal chart is exactly this span: a distant wish, carefully placed into the life right in front of him.

item.title: HBS Prep | Operations: AI-First Snack — Count checking as part of efficiency
item.description: This time, the prep material isn't a long case about a company. The professor gave us three questions: how I like to use AI, how it will change business over the next 6–18 months, and how I want employees to use it.

item.title: HBS Prep | Negotiation: Thirteen Days — Leave the other side a way to follow through
item.description: Thirteen Days — A Memoir of the Cuban Missile Crisis.

item.title: HBS Prep | Marketing: Starbucks Korea — Who Actually Read That Copy?
item.description: Starbucks Korea’s Tank Day: When the Machines Forgot.

item.title: HBS Prep | Management Control: A Letter from Prison — Time Is Part of the Facts Too
item.description: The contracts were real, the products were delivered, and the cash came in. So one manager came to believe that booking revenue a few days early was fundamentally different from the more sensational financial scandals. This case makes you see again that time itself is part of the facts.

item.title: HBS Prep | Strategy: Golden Goose — How to Grow Without Losing the Brand's Reason for Being
item.description: A company that sells distressed sneakers has grown to hundreds of millions of euros in revenue. The next question is how to keep growing while holding on to the reason customers wanted to walk in the door in the first place.

item.title: HBS Prep | Strategy: Breezm — How customization becomes a repeatable business
item.description: A pair of glasses you wear on your face every day can have the right prescription, a great look, and a badly balanced weight all at the same time. Breezm starts from this very specific discomfort and tries to reorganize how glasses are made and served.

item.title: HBS Prep | Leadership: Unspeakable — Saying Clearly the Things That Are Hard to Talk About
item.description: Unspeakable: The Taboo Topics We Avoid and How to Talk About Them, and Note on Difficult Conversations in the Family Enterprise.

item.description: Mercado Bitcoin: M&A, IPO, or Series B?.

item.title: HBS Prep | Finance: GeBBS — Who takes the helm after you sell the equity
item.description: GeBBS Healthcare Solutions: Did You Ever Have to Make Up Your Mind?.

item.title: HBS Prep | Global Markets: Equity Group — How much public responsibility can a company take on?
item.description: “A Marshall Plan for Africa”: James Mwangi and Equity Group Holdings.

item.title: HBS Notes | Finance: Nantucket Nectars — Valuation starts with asking who the buyer is
item.description: class discussion of Nantucket Nectars: The Exit.

item.title: HBS Prep | Leadership: Lisa Su and AMD — Focus and delivery in a crisis
item.description: Why does a company that once made excellent products end up in trouble? And how does the person who takes it over reorganize the capabilities that still exist into a path that actually works?

item.title: HBS Prep | Finance: Slater & Gordon — What kind of capital growth needs
item.description: Creating the First Public Law Firm: The IPO of Slater & Gordon Limited.

item.title: HBS Prep | Global Markets: India — How Development Can Reach the Many
item.description: A country that can already land on the Moon, export software and build a digital payments system at enormous scale still has to answer a plain question: how do these capabilities turn into a life that most people can actually live?

item.title: HBS Prep | Control: Lehman Brothers — Why paper compliance couldn't stop the window dressing
item.description: In another class the same day, Frances Frei asks whether service is something you design. This class asks about control — the audit firm, the law firm, management: what role did each of them play? In this story, every piece of paper is in order. What's missing is the number behind the paper.

item.title: HBS Prep | Strategy: KLog.co — Should growth go deep first, or go wide first?
item.description: KLog.co – Charting the Course of its Future.

item.title: HBS Prep | Global Markets: The Atlantic and OpenAI — Should Content Be Sold to the Models?
item.description: The last piece asked whether the silicon shield is a protection or a weak spot. This one swings the camera from wafers to a magazine. What gets taken for training here isn't production capacity — it's sentences.

item.title: HBS Prep | Global Markets: Taiwan Semiconductors — Is the Silicon Shield a Protection or a Weak Spot?
item.description: Taiwan, Semiconductors, and a “New Cold War”?

item.title: HBS Prep | Operations: Commerce Bank — Service Is Designed
item.description: The last piece, on Spyder, asked how ownership rewrites a company's value. This one asks something else: is service excellence designed, or improvised on a Friday afternoon? The story takes place on Halloween 2002 — at a bank that calls its branches stores and its customers fans, and that has just let its managers juggle in the lobby.

item.title: HBS Prep | Finance: Spyder Active Sports — How Ownership Changes Value
item.description: The previous piece, Nantucket Nectars, was about the seller — a company is worth the most in the year someone else needs you. This one is about the seller too, but the question flips over: the same company, with a different shareholder, isn't worth the same number. Not because the model changed, but because the people showing up to work next Monday changed.

item.description: New WOW at Equitable (A): A New Way of Working.

item.title: HBS Prep | Innovation Case: Roaring Out of Recession — In a recession, the fastest to cut jobs lose the most; save on process and spend on customers to expand against the wind
item.description: Roaring Out of Recession and Investing in Growth Through Uncertainty.

item.title: HBS Prep | Finance Case: Nantucket Nectars — A company is worth the most in the year someone else needs you; don't wait for the year you need cash to sell
item.description: The last few pieces were all about how to build a company — Olay took its brand apart and put it back together, Belden transformed while profits were still rising, Bajaj guarded the gap between two purchases. This one runs the other way: the company has been built, and two founders in their early thirties have to decide whether to sell, to whom, and how. It's a story about "what it's worth," and…

item.title: HBS Notes | Marketing Case: Olay — The Promise Can Change; Condescension Can't Stay
item.description: Before class, I cast my vote for "fewer and clearer." Don't sell the brand. Don't chase 19-year-olds' acne. Cut the overlapping claims on the shelf and tell the red jar's story clearly. Swap "anti-aging" for a line that doesn't frighten anyone.
